newsitem.title: USA: Poll says most see U.S. bankruptcy system as too lenient.
newsitem.headline: Poll says most see U.S. bankruptcy system as too lenient.

text.p: At a time when Americans are declaring bankruptcy in record numbers, most people believe the system for handling such cases is too lenient, according to a poll released Monday.

"By overwhelming majorities, Americans say it is too easy to file for personal bankruptcy and they want those who do file to repay as much of their outstanding debt as they can," the Bankruptcy Issues Working Group said in a statement.
The group is a coalition representing the major credit card companies, Visa and Mastercard, and the banks that issue the cards.

A poll by Opinion Research Corp. that the coalition released showed that three-quarters of those surveyed said people should have to prove they need bankruptcy relief before they are allowed to have their debts written off -- something the current system does not require.
"Only 16 percent favour the status quo in which 'individuals should be the ones to decide whether they need to file bankruptcy and write off their debts,'" the coalition said.
The national survey of 1,011 adults was conducted Nov. 14-17.
A large majority, 83 percent, advocated requiring people to pay back at least some of their debt if they can.
Fourteen percent of those polled, however, favoured giving people a fresh start by forgiving virtually all of their debts.
The survey comes as data released Monday by the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts showed the annual rate of bankruptcy filings jumped 26 percent to 1.11 million in the third quarter.
In the second quarter, the annual rate of filings topped the 1 million mark for the first time.

That statistic was highlighted last week in a speech by Federal Reserve Gov. Lawrence Lindsey, who has among several officials voicing concern about the amount of debt Americans have taken on in recent years.

On Friday, the Federal Reserve reported that consumers again picked up the pace on credit buying as outstanding consumer instalment credit rose in October by $2.2 billion at a 2.3 percent annual rate. It fell a revised $700 million in September at a 0.8 percent annual rate.
Lindsey has called attention in particular to high debt levels among people in the middle- to upper-middle-income brackets.
The Fed official has also warned that high and rising debt levels suggested that bankruptcy filings could increase to even higher levels.

While suggesting that Americans might want to see a more stringent bankruptcy system, the poll also indicated that most people are not all that familiar with the system or with ways they might avoid ending up in it.

More than half of those polled admitted they "do not know very much" about the bankruptcy system. Upwards of six in 10 said they had "heard about, but don't know much about" organisations that provide counselling to financially strapped people to help them avoid having to file for bankruptcy.
